title: Explaining is how you find out whether you understand

blocks.html: Checked against the sources as they stood on 2026-09-25.

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
People feel they understand how things work in far more detail than they do. Rozenblit and Keil named this the illusion of explanatory depth in 2002.

It is measured in three steps. A person rates how well they understand something. They write out a detailed, step-by-step explanation of how it works. Then they rate their understanding again.

In Rozenblit and Keil’s first study, 16 graduate students rated 48 things taken from books on how things work. Each then explained four devices, such as a zipper or a flush toilet, and rated again. The ratings fell after explaining.

The drop has held up. In a second study, 33 undergraduates showed the same pattern. When students were warned at the start that they would have to write explanations, the drop was smaller, but it did not go away. The drop was large for devices and natural processes, small for facts such as capital cities, and absent for procedures and for the plots of films.

Expertise does not reliably remove the illusion either. A later study from the same laboratory found that people with more education show it on topics from their own subject.

Two study techniques put explaining to work. In self-explanation, a learner explains how new information relates to what they already know, or explains the steps they take while solving a problem. In elaborative interrogation, a learner works out why a stated fact is true. A 2013 review by Dunlosky and colleagues rated both of moderate utility, below the high utility of practice testing.

Self-explanation has helped across different materials, a wide range of ages, and tests of memory, understanding and transfer to new problems. Almost all the studies of both tested learners within minutes, and few were run outside the laboratory.

blocks.label: In plain terms
blocks.html:
Ask yourself whether you understand how a ceiling fan works, and you will probably say yes. Now write down, step by step, what happens between pressing the switch and the blades turning. Then ask yourself the first question again. Your answer is likely to come down.

That drop is the illusion of explanatory depth. You felt you understood. Trying to explain showed you where you do not.

The illusion lives in “how does it work” and “why”. In one study, people judged their knowledge of everyday procedures, such as how to bake chocolate chip cookies from scratch or tie a bow tie, about right. The steps for weighing a child may behave the same way; nobody has tested it. Ask why each step is there, and you are asking how something works.

So use explaining as a check. When a student nods, ask them to explain the step.

blocks.alt: Two bars: with "Why is this true?" prompts, 76% correct; reading only, 69% correct.
blocks.caption: One introductory biology class reading a textbook passage on human digestion. Students who met a “Why is this true?” prompt about every 150 words got 76% of 105 true-or-false questions right. Students who read without prompts got 69%. Guessing alone would score about 50%. The test was not reported as delayed.

blocks.alt: Two bars: 32 minutes spent reading with "Why is this true?" prompts, 28 minutes reading only.
blocks.caption: What the prompts cost in the same class: 32 minutes of reading with “Why is this true?” prompts against 28 without, 4 minutes more for 7 more percentage points correct.

blocks.label: Illustration 1
blocks.html:
Start with yourself. Pick something you use every day and believe you understand: how a pressure cooker cooks dal faster than an open pan. Give yourself a mark from 1 to 7 for how well you understand it. 1 means you have almost no idea and 7 means you could explain every part. That is the scale Rozenblit and Keil gave their students. Write the mark down.

Now write out the explanation as a chain of steps, each one following from the one before. Book 0’s section on premise and inference (Book 0, F4) gave you the test: each step has to follow from the last. Wherever you find yourself writing “and then somehow”, a step is missing.

Mark yourself again, from 1 to 7. If the second mark is lower, you have just met the illusion.

Open Rozenblit and Keil, “The misunderstood limits of folk science”, Cognitive Science 2002, at https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3062901/. Search the page for genuine surprise.

many participants reported genuine surprise and new humility at how much less they knew than they originally thought

These were graduate students who had just tried to explain a zipper or a flush toilet. Now search for extreme warning.

Importantly, the drop was still significant—the illusion held even with the extreme warning.

Here the students had been told at the start that they would have to write explanations. The drop was smaller than without the warning, and it was still there. Now search for cookbook.

People appear to be quite accurate in assessing their own knowledge of “cookbook” procedures in contrast to their knowledge of how things work.

This tells you where to aim the check. Say you will teach a batch of MBBS students to measure a child’s height next week. The steps in the manual are a procedure, and you probably know them about as well as you think. Now write, from memory, why each step is there, and what goes wrong in the reading if it is skipped. That is a question about how something works. Mark every place you stall. That list is your reading for the evening.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html: The paper plots its students’ mean ratings and does not print them, so you cannot compare the size of your own drop with theirs. A lower second mark tells you that you overrated yourself. It does not tell you what the right explanation is. A smooth explanation can still be wrong, and only checking it against a good source shows that. The students explained devices. Nobody in these studies tested the reasons behind the steps of a clinical method, so treat the height example as a place to look, not a measured case.

blocks.label: Illustration 2
blocks.html:
Now turn explaining into something your learners do. You are taking a batch of MBBS students through a textbook passage on human digestion.

Dunlosky and colleagues describe a class study of this kind, by Smith and colleagues in 2010. Open their review at https://doi.org/10.1177/1529100612453266 and search for Why is this true. Undergraduates in an introductory biology course read a long passage on human digestion from their course textbook.

For half of the students, 21 elaborative interrogation prompts were interspersed throughout the text (roughly one prompt per 150 words)

Each prompt was a statement from the text followed by “Why is this true?” The other half read at their own pace without prompts. Everyone then answered 105 true-or-false questions, none of them the same as the prompts.

Group Minutes spent reading Questions correct
“Why is this true?” prompts 32 76%
Reading only 28 69%

Guessing alone would score about 50% on a true-or-false test.

Work out what the prompts bought, and what they cost.

76 minus 69 = 7 percentage points more correct
32 minus 28 = 4 minutes more reading

To use it, pick the statements in your passage that carry the mechanism. After each one, write “Why is this true?” Your students answer in writing. Then they check the answer against the text, or with you, because an explanation that is wrong and left unchecked can hurt learning.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html: This is one class, one passage and a true-or-false test. The account does not say the test was taken days later, and almost all studies of this technique tested within minutes, so the 7 points say nothing about what lasted. Prompts spread thinly, one every page or two, have shrunk the benefit or reversed it. Learners who know little about a subject may gain less from “why” questions.

points.html: A learner who nods, or says “yes, understood”, has told you how they feel, not what they can do. Ask them to explain the step in their own words, aloud or on paper.
Before you teach a topic, write your explanation out from memory, and read up on the places where you stall.
When you ask learners to explain, have them check the explanation against the text or against you. A poor explanation, left unchecked, can hurt learning (Weinstein and colleagues).
Asking someone to list the steps of a procedure may not show you the illusion. In one study, people judged their knowledge of everyday procedures about right.

Do not claim that “why” questions or self-explanation produce lasting learning. Only a few studies tested after a delay, and their results were promising. Test your own learners days later before you say they worked.

Self-explanation took 30% to 100% more time in the few self-paced studies that reported it. The “why” prompts in the biology class took 32 minutes against 28 for reading alone. Weigh fewer problems explained against more problems solved.

blocks.prompt: A first-year resident tells you: “I read the chapter on anthropometry, body measurement, twice last night. I understood all of it, so I can take the MBBS batch on Monday.” You have ten minutes and a whiteboard. Explain why “I understood it” is not yet evidence. Then give them one thing to do tonight instead of a third reading.
blocks.answer:
Start with the mechanism. Feeling that you understand is a rating you give yourself, and people rate their understanding of how things work higher than it is. When they then write out a full explanation and rate themselves again, the second rating is lower. Being warned that the explanation would be asked for made the drop smaller, not absent. Being well educated in the subject does not stop it either.

Then the whiteboard. Do not ask only for the steps of a measurement; in one study, people judged their knowledge of everyday procedures about right. Ask why. Take the height measurement, step by step as the chapter gives it. For each step, ask why it is there and what happens to the reading if it is skipped. Let the resident talk, and mark where they stop or say “and then basically”.

Then the task for tonight. Close the book. Write out, from memory, the explanation they would give the batch, as a chain of steps with the reason for each. Mark every place they stall. Open the book only for those places. Writing it from memory is also retrieval practice, so the same hour checks the understanding and strengthens it.

Close with the limit. A smooth explanation can still be wrong, so the check against the book is part of the task, not an extra.
